content:
{'translated': 'There is a well-known saying in photography circles: the best camera is the one you have with you at the time. The iPhone is of course the camera that most people carry around, and for shooting kids, social events and other scenarios, this is clearly a huge advantage. But a recent video project led me to discover another benefit.'}

{'translated': 'I really enjoy strolling around London in the evening, and often use my iPhone to take photos and short videos. At first it was simply to satisfy a craving to shoot, and only later did I realise that these short clips were perfect as cutaway b-roll footage for a video project…'}

{'translated': 'My current project is experimental in nature — it is being used to test the viability of Cinematic Mode, which is why I lamented earlier that it seems the company has stopped developing it. Once the project is finished next week I will share more with everyone.'}

{'translated': 'I planned to follow a very specific format, requiring short landscape cutaway shots to be edited into the interviews. In principle these clips could have been filmed anywhere in London, but because the main scene is by the river, I really wanted all the cutaways to be of the Thames. I needed four clips — I scrolled through the videos on my iPhone for a while and already found suitable material.'}

{'translated': 'The clip above also highlights another appealing aspect. In case there are people in the frame who might be recognisable, I will walk over to them afterwards, let them have a look at the footage, and then ask for their consent to use it. (This is not a legal requirement in the UK, but I think it is a matter of courtesy.) Quite often they will actively ask me to send them the clip. If the other person uses an iPhone, AirDrop gets it done quickly; for Android users, WhatsApp serves as a fallback.'}

{'translated': "The iPhone's image stabilisation feature is really extremely useful, especially since I did not originally set out to shoot anything — these were all handheld, captured spontaneously when I came across a nice scene while out for a walk. I do try to use walls, railings or lamp posts to steady the device, but generally speaking, the footage comes out very stable as is, honestly indistinguishable from what you'd get with a tripod. (If I deliberately plan to shoot while out for a walk, I will also bring a small GorillaPod tripod along.)"}

{'translated': "Another major advantage of the iPhone is its 'point-and-shoot' nature. If I had to manually adjust exposure, white balance, ND filters and so on, I probably wouldn't want the hassle, especially when walking around with other people — fiddling about takes too much time and ends up disturbing the people I'm with. But if I only need to ask someone to wait for around twenty seconds, it won't feel like a chore."}

{'translated': 'If I want to stay in one spot for a while, shooting time-lapse video on the iPhone is also incredibly easy. Once you start recording, you can stop at any time, and the iPhone will automatically adjust to give you a clip of just the right length. At the flat where I used to live, I would often prop the iPhone by the window, start a time-lapse recording whenever there was a sunset, and then get on with my own work. A few of those clips also became excellent b-roll material for the video project.'}

{'translated': "Of course, if you zoom in pixel by pixel, the limitations of the iPhone's small sensor do start to show, and this is especially obvious in low-light conditions. But nowadays most YouTube viewers watch videos on their phones or laptops, and for these uses the footage is more than adequate."}

{'translated': 'Whether the footage shot in Cinematic Mode is of equally high quality is somewhat harder to say — next week everyone will be able to help judge. But overall, I am genuinely amazed at having such a powerful camera tucked away in my pocket, ready to use whenever and wherever I pull it out.'}
